pip from its repository. One command per dataset reruns the audit and the head experiment and then the table and figure scripts. Every run writes a manifest that records the code commit and configuration together with hashes of the data (Appendix D). The probe audit of 50,000 images with K = 500 permutations took 11 min on a laptop CPU.

4. Experiments

The synthetic benchmark addresses the first question of the Introduction on data where the truth is known: it checks that the probe and the secondary detectors hold their false positive rate, and it measures their power. The clinical audits then apply the test to common frozen encoders on two chest radiograph cohorts, for sex, age and race. The classification-head experiment addresses the second question: it trains heads on confounded CheXpert data and asks whether the audit score predicts how much they rely on the attribute, and whether four mitigation methods reduce that reliance. A planted image marker supplies a shortcut with known ground truth, and CelebA is a non-medical check. Table 3 lists which method is used in which experiment. Seeds and run manifests are described in Appendix D.

4.1. Synthetic benchmark

The synthetic data make the answer known. The task label is Y ∼ Bernoulli(0.5) and the attribute satisfies P (A = Y ) = ρ for ρ equal to 0.5, 0.7 or 0.9, so A and Y are distinct variables whose correlation we control. Embeddings have d standard normal dimensions. The task signal sits in its own block of dimensions. The attribute signal sits in a separate block and comes in three forms. In the linear mean shift the two groups differ by exactly δ standard deviations (each shifted by ±δ/2, so δ is Cohen's d in each attribute dimension). The nonlinear XOR form leaves both group means at zero and carries the attribute in the sign of the product of two dimensions. Under the variance shift the groups have equal means and unequal variances (Appendix E). We varied δ ∈ {0, 0.2, 0.5, 0.8, 1.2, 2.0}, n ∈ {200, 1000} and d ∈ {128, 512}, with 10 seeds per configuration. The ground truth is that I(E; A | Y ) > 0 exactly when δ > 0. At δ = 0 with ρ = 0.9, the embedding predicts A through Y but carries no extra information, which is the case a conditional test has to get right.

A mean shift in a few dimensions is a simplification. Shortcut signal in real encoders is likely spread across many dimensions and may be nonlinear. The XOR and variance variants were added to test whether each detector can see signals that leave group means unchanged, and the planted image marker (Section 4.3) tests the pipeline on a shortcut that passes through a real encoder. For each detector and variant we report sensitivity (flag rate at δ > 0) and specificity (one minus flag rate at δ = 0), the operating characteristics of the descriptive count k for k = 1, . . . , 6, the pairwise correlation of detector flags, and the effective number of independent detectors computed from the eigenvalues of that correlation matrix [55, 56].

4.2. Clinical cohorts CheXpert.

We used the first 2,000 images streamed from a public Hugging Face mirror of the CheXpert training set [57]. These follow the order of the official train.csv, which is not random. They come from 477 patients, and 423 are lateral views. The mirror itself has no patient identifiers, so we joined each image by its path to the official train.csv, which gives the patient identifier, sex, age, view and findings, and took race per patient from the CheXpert demographics file. Images without a demographics record, or with race recorded as unknown or refused (217 images), are left out of the race analyses. Native Hawaiian or Pacific Islander (24 images) is its own group and counts as non-White in the binary split. All cross-validation and permutation on CheXpert is grouped by patient. The audit task is Pneumothorax, with Y = 1 for a positive label and Y = 0 otherwise (prevalence 10.9%). Y = 0 covers 584 negative, 23 uncertain and 1,175 blank labels, and Table F.7 repeats the audit on the 802 images with a definite label.

MIMIC-CXR.

We used 1,491 subjects from MIMIC-CXR [58], one image per subject, so ordinary cross-validation is already patient-level. The images are a coreset of 1,999 images drawn for an earlier embedding project by stratified sampling on pathology labels (strategy "PathologyStratified-Clean", seed 0, of the public embedding dataset https://huggingface.co/datasets/MITCriticalData/qml-mimic-cxr-embeddings, which also provides the coreset strata used in [59]). All are frontal (AP or PA) views. Rows without a linked hospital admission outcome were removed. The task is in-hospital mortality of the linked admission (hospital_expire_flag in MIMIC-IV [60]), prevalence 6.0%. Mortality is an outcome that depends on many factors outside the image, and no radiological finding defines it.

Encoders.

All encoders were used frozen, with their published weights and no fine-tuning on either cohort. Table 4 separates architecture from pretraining. Some public encoders were pretrained on corpora that include CheXpert or MIMIC-CXR images. RAD-DINO [61] publishes its list of training images, and all 2000 CheXpert images in our sample (477 patients) and 1479 of the 1491 MIMIC-CXR images are on it. RAD-DINO is self-supervised, so it saw these images without their labels or attributes, and its scores here describe an encoder that has seen the audited images. We did not train any encoder, so no patient in our analysis was used in a training step we controlled. All seven CheXpert embeddings are extracted with code in the repository from pinned public checkpoints. In the first submission four of them (ViT-B/32, DINOv2, RAD-DINO, MedSigLIP) were arrays stored without their extraction code, which could not be reproduced exactly. We re-extracted those four from the same images, and every CheXpert result here uses the re-extracted arrays. The extraction code reproduces the stored ViT-B/16 array, whose code was kept, to cosine 1.000, and Table F.6 compares the old and new arrays for the other four. The MIMIC-CXR embeddings come from the same public dataset: the CLS token of ViT-Base-Patch16-224 and ViT-Base-Patch32-224, RAD-DINO, and MedSigLIP-448. The dataset's documentation names google/siglip-so400m-patch14-384 for the last one, but re-embedding 50 of its images with google/medsiglip-448 reproduced the stored vectors (cosine 1.000 for every image), while the general-purpose SigLIP So400m checkpoint did not (median 0.15).

4.3. Classification-head experiment

The audit measures potential, and to measure use and harm we trained classification heads on frozen CheXpert embeddings, for every encoder, with A equal to sex and then age, and three tasks: Pneumothorax, Pleural Effusion and Cardiomegaly. For these tasks, uncertain and blank labels are dropped per task. Train and test sets are disjoint at patient level (a two-fold split grouped by patient and stratified on (A, Y )), and each cell is repeated with 10 seeds. Reliance on A is measured two ways: the gaps in true and false positive rate between groups on the test set, and the drop in test AUROC relative to a head trained on an unconfounded subsample of the same size. We also report the mean absolute change in the head's output when the attribute direction is removed from the test embeddings (output shift). Appendix C explains why it is not used as a measure of reliance. That direction is the difference of the two group means after centring each Y stratum, estimated on the training pool. Each test embedding x is replaced by x-((x-m) ⊤ u) u, with u the unit direction and m the training mean, and the confounded head is applied again. We also report the head's AUROC separately on test images where A and Y agree with the training correlation (aligned) and where they disagree (misaligned), as in Kina and Petersen [14]. To check that the result does not depend on the linear head, the reliance measures are repeated on the same splits and seeds with a multilayer perceptron at the scikit-learn defaults (one hidden layer of 256 ReLU units, Adam with learning rate 10 -3 , L2 weight 10 -3 and up to 500 iterations).

Confounded training.

Audit score against reliance. Across encoder, attribute and task cells we compute the Spearman rank correlation between the conditional probe score, computed on all labelled images of the task, and each reliance measure, with a bootstrap confidence interval over cells. The cells are not independent, since the seven encoders embed the same images and the attributes and tasks reuse the same patients. We therefore also report an interval from resampling whole encoders and the partial correlation given attribute and task. With seven encoders this interval is itself imprecise.

Mitigation.

The three embedding-level mitigations of Section 3.6 and their controls are fitted on the confounded training embeddings and applied to the training and test embeddings, after which the head is retrained and the audit rerun on the test half of the patients. For DFR only the head is refit. Because the test half is smaller, the probe score before mitigation is lower than in Table 8, which uses all labelled images. The TPR gap before mitigation is the mean over the first 3 of the 10 seeds. Before and after each method we report the audit score and the task AUROC, together with the TPR gap.

Planted marker. To test the pipeline on a shortcut with known ground truth that passes through a real encoder, we stamped a white square (27 by 27 pixels, intensity 255, at the same position on every image, its corner at 30% of the width and height) into the CheXpert images at 320 pixels on the shorter side, before the encoder's resizing to 224, embedded the images with the torchvision ResNet-50, and audited with the marker as the attribute and Pneumothorax as the task. For the audit, images with Y = 1 received the marker at rate r = 0.5. For the head, the training images with Y = 1 received it at rate 0.9. Images with Y = 0 never carried the marker in training. Patients were split in half for the head, and test images received the marker on a random half regardless of Y , so a head that ignores the marker shows no gap. The experiment was repeated with 10 seeds.

4.4. CelebA

CelebA [62] was used as a non-medical check. We extracted ResNet-50 embeddings (2,048 dimensions) from 10,000 images drawn at random with a fixed seed from the 202,599 and audited A = Male given each of three tasks, Y ∈ {Blond hair, Heavy makeup, Attractive}, which are known to correlate with Male in this dataset. Images are grouped by celebrity identity for crossvalidation and permutation.

5. Results

>Results

5.1. Synthetic benchmark

The conditional permutation null held its nominal level. Pooled over all null configurations, the detectors rejected in 0.02 (conditional probe) to 0.08 (bias direction) of runs at p < 0.05, the level at which the probe is judged, and after Benjamini-Hochberg across the five secondary detectors no secondary detector exceeded 0.03 (Table E.1). The grid has 40 null data sets for each ρ, and at ρ = 0.9 the geometric and statistical detectors rejected in 0.17 and 0.12 of them, and the bias-direction detector in 0.15. A permutation test is exact under H 0 whatever the statistic, so we drew 500 further null data sets at ρ = 0.9, n = 1000 and d = 128, the grid setting with the most rejections. There the three rates were 0.05, 0.03 and 0.06 (HBAC 0.07, frequency 0.04, probe 0.03), so the higher grid values reflect how few grid data sets there are. Conditioning mattered most when A and Y were strongly correlated. At ρ = 0.9 and δ = 0, where the embedding predicts A only through Y , an unconditional probe rejected the null in 0.95 of data sets and the conditional probe in 0.03.

For the linear signal, the probe's sensitivity was 0.16 at δ = 0.2, 0.62 at δ = 0.5 and 0.87 at δ = 0.8 (Table 5, Figure 2). The frequency, statistical and geometric detectors had similar power, and HBAC had much less.

Every detector missed the nonlinear and variance-shift signals. At δ = 2.0 on the XOR variant, sensitivity was 0.02 for the probe, 0.02 for HBAC and 0.03 for the statistical detector, and on the variance-shift variant the same three were 0.02, 0.02 and 0.02. For every detector and every δ, sensitivity on these two variants stayed at or near the level of its false positive rate under the null. All six statistics respond to differences in group means, directly or through a linear model, and neither variant changes the means.

Over the whole grid the detectors' flags were strongly correlated (mean pairwise correlation 0.76, Table E.2), with an effective number of independent Table 5: Synthetic benchmark: specificity at δ = 0 and sensitivity at each δ > 0 (Cohen's d), per detector and signal variant. Most of this correlation comes from the effect size, since every detector flags more often as δ grows. For the linear signal at a fixed effect size the effective number was 3.0 at δ = 0.2, 2.2 at δ = 0.5 and 3.0 at δ = 0.8, and 3.7 under the null. Requiring more detectors to agree lowered sensitivity at every effect size without a useful gain in specificity, because the probe alone already had a false positive rate of 0.02 at p < 0.05 (Figure 3).

5.2. Clinical audit Patient-level calibration.

CheXpert has several images per patient. To see whether that matters, we drew a fake binary attribute at patient level, unrelated to the images, 30 times on the RAD-DINO embeddings (Table F.3).

With image-level permutation and ordinary cross-validation, the conditional probe rejected the null in 1.00 of draws, and so did every secondary detector: images of the same patient look alike and share the fake label, so a probe can match them across folds. With patient-level permutation and folds grouped by patient, the probe rejected in 0.00 of draws (0 of 30; the 95% upper bound on its false positive rate is 0.11, so the control rules out the leakage rather than estimating that rate precisely). All CheXpert re- sults below use the patient-level version. Grouping also lowered the observed probe scores. For sex on ResNet-50, for example, the AUROC was 0.841 grouped vs 0.887 plain.

Audit results.

Every encoder carried attribute information beyond the task label, for every attribute. Tables 6 and 7 give the conditional probe AUROC with its interval and p-value and the continuous score of each secondary detector for every encoder and attribute, and Figure 4 shows the same scores.

Tables F.11 to F.16 in Appendix F list, for every detector and cell, the statistic, the mean and SD of its permutation null, the raw p-value and, for the secondary detectors, the BH-adjusted q-value. The conditional probe rejected H 0 in 21 of 21 CheXpert cells and in 12 of 12 MIMIC-CXR cells. Adjusting the probe's p-values across the 21 CheXpert cells by Benjamini-Hochberg leaves all 21 below 0.05 (largest q = 0.022), and the same holds across the 12 MIMIC-CXR cells. The MIMIC-CXR ViT-B/32 row uses the file rebuilt from the source (Table F.5 and the comparison with the submitted pipeline below). Sex had the largest potential, with a conditional probe AUROC of 0.84 to 0.99 on CheXpert and 0.93 to 1.00 on MIMIC-CXR, where RAD-DINO reached 1.00 (95% CI 1.00 to 1.00). For age the ranges were 0.67 to 0.83 on CheXpert and 0.80 to 0.89 on MIMIC-CXR. Race differed between the cohorts: 0.57 to 0.61 on CheXpert, where the MedSigLIP cell was the weakest and is flagged by the primary test alone (p = 0.022, none of its five secondary detectors flagged). Had the probe been adjusted together with the secondary detectors, it would not have been (q = 0.13), and this is the only cell on which the two rules differ. Race potential was higher at 0.66 to 0.76 on MIMIC-CXR. MedSigLIP-448, re-extracted for this revision, was among the strongest CheXpert encoders for sex and age (0.97 and 0.80). The unidentified array used under that name in the first submission had been the weakest for every attribute.

Stability of the race result.

Table F.8 subsamples the non-White group to fixed sizes on RAD-DINO, ten draws per size. On CheXpert the probe rejected in 0.10 of draws with 25 non-White images and in 0.80 with 400, and its AUROC varied widely between draws (SD 0.16 at the smallest size). On MIMIC-CXR the rejection rate was 0.80 at 25 images and 1.00 at 400. The CheXpert race signal is weak: the probe rejected in 7 of 10 draws with 200 non-White images and in 8 of 10 with 400, but rarely with 100 or fewer, whereas the MIMIC-CXR signal is detected with 50. Keeping race groups with at least 50 images as separate groups (White, Black and Asian on CheXpert, and White and Black on MIMIC-CXR, which has 38 Asian subjects) gave somewhat higher AUROCs than the binary split (Table F.1), and four age bins gave somewhat lower ones than the binary split (Table F.2).

Sensitivity of the audit.

Table F.7 repeats the CheXpert probe with three changes. On the 1577 frontal images alone no AUROC moved by more than 0.03, and 21 of 21 cells were significant, against 21 in the main audit. Keeping only the 802 images with a definite Pneumothorax label, as in the head experiment, no AUROC moved by more than 0.06, and 20 of 21 cells had p < 0.05, with MedSigLIP race, the weakest cell of the main audit, the one exception. Setting the probe's regularisation to C = 0.1 or C = 10 changed the significance decision in 0 of 42 cells. With the arrays used in the first submission the four re-extracted encoders gave AUROCs up to 0.29 away from the main result, almost all of it from the unidentified MedSigLIP array. Appending the squared coordinates to the probe's features changed the decision in 0 of 33 clinical cells and raised the AUROC by at most 0.02 (Appendix E, Table E.4).

What the embeddings cluster on.

To see whether the embeddings carry structure that the named attributes do not explain, we compared k-means clusters (k = 8) with all recorded metadata (Table F.9). On both cohorts the clusters followed image acquisition most closely: the strongest association on CheXpert was with AP/PA and on MIMIC-CXR with view (AP/PA), and on CheXpert the frontal-versus-lateral view had a mean normalised mutual information of 0.378 with the clusters. Support devices came next on CheXpert (0.068, range 0.052 to 0.103). Sex, age and race were weakly associated with the clusters even where the probe recovered them well, so these attributes are encoded in directions that do not dominate the overall structure of the embedding.

Comparison with the submitted pipeline.

Rerunning the submitted 13-method pipeline with only the flag reader fixed changed its clinical tables (Table F.10). The statistical, geometric and GCE detectors, which the submitted tables showed as never flagging, flagged in every CheXpert cell once their results were read correctly, and the mean agreement count on CheXpert rose from 7.0 to 9.4 of 13 (MIMIC-CXR: 5.2 to 7.5). The identical age and race rows of the submitted CheXpert table, present for 6 of 7 encoders, came from detectors that fitted on the task label and so returned the same output for every attribute. These comparisons describe the old pipeline only, and none of its outputs is used elsewhere in this paper. One input of the submitted pipeline was also replaced. The submitted MIMIC-CXR ViT-B/32 file failed two independent checks (Table F.5): it held the first 1,491 rows of its source, taken before rows without an outcome were removed. Its similarity structure matched no other encoder (largest Spearman correlation 0.006), and its sex probe was at chance (AUROC 0.50, against 0.93 for ViT-B/16 on the same images). The file rebuilt from the source passed both (0.499 and 0.94), and every MIMIC-CXR result in this paper uses it.

5.3. Classification-head experiment

Across the 42 encoder, attribute and task cells, heads trained on confounded data relied on the attribute (Table 8). The mean TPR gap between groups on the balanced test set was 0.19. On test images where attribute and label disagreed with the training correlation, the head's AUROC was 0.61, against 0.85 where they agreed. A head trained on unconfounded data of the same size scored 0.75 and 0.77. The drop in overall test AUROC was smaller (mean 0.02), because the balanced test set mixes aligned and misaligned images. Calibration error was similar for the two groups (0.248 and 0.245).

The audit score correlated with the size of this reliance: across cells, the Spearman correlation between the conditional probe AUROC and the TPR gap was 0.60 (95% CI 0.33 to 0.79, or 0.31 to 0.80 when whole encoders are resampled, and partial correlation given attribute and task 0.63). With the FPR gap it was 0.28 (p = 0.072), and with the AUROC drop 0.72 (Figure 5). Within attributes the correlation with the TPR gap was 0.74 for sex (interval 0.19 to 0.94 when encoders are resampled, p < 0.001) and 0.19 for age (-0.29 to 0.57, p = 0.417), so the relation was clear across encoders for sex and uncertain within age. Leaving out any one encoder, the correlation ranged from 0.50 (without RAD-DINO) to 0.68, and leaving out any one task from 0.45 (without Pneumothorax) to 0.73. With the mean of the permutation null subtracted from each probe score, which removes the part a head could get from Y alone, the correlation was 0.57 (0.75 within sex, 0.09 within age). With a multilayer perceptron head (one hidden layer of 256 units) trained on the same splits the correlation was 0.53 (interval 0.20 to 0.76 when encoders are resampled), 0.70 within sex and 0.09 within age, and the two heads' TPR gaps correlated at 0.96 across cells.

With race as the attribute (White against non-White), the probe AU-ROCs spanned only 0.52 to 0.65, the confounded heads showed no consistent gap, and the correlation across the 21 cells was 0.03 (Table C.2 in Appendix C).

Mitigation.

At the package defaults, none of the three mitigations that alter the embedding reduced the head's TPR gap by more than 0.01 beyond its control, and only contrastive debiasing lowered the probe score beyond its control, by a small margin (Table 9). Paired by cell and seed, the methodminus-control differences in TPR gap were -0.01 for adversarial debiasing (-0.03 to 0.01 when whole encoders are resampled), 0.00 for contrastive debi-asing (-0.03 to 0.02) and -0.01 for masking (-0.03 to -0.00); RAD-DINO was the one encoder on which all three lowered the gap, by about 0.06 relative to its controls. With adversarial debiasing the mean conditional probe AUROC changed by -0.09, and the number of audits with a significant probe went from 123 to 100 of 126. The control network without the adversary changed it by -0.09, which leaves -0.01 for the adversary itself. The contrastive debiasing method lowered the probe further, a change of -0.16 against -0.12 for its control, a difference of -0.04. Significant audits went from 123 to 70, and to 85 for its control. Relative to their controls, the adversarial and contrastive methods changed the task AUROC by 0.00 and 0.00 and the confounded head's TPR gap by -0.01 and 0.00. Most of the lower audit score came from passing the embeddings through a small learned debiasing network, and in every case the confounded head found the attribute signal that remained.

Masking the top 5% of attribute dimensions barely moved the probe (-0.01, against 0.00 for random dimensions), because the attribute is spread over many dimensions, and relative to its control it changed the TPR gap by -0.01. Refitting the head on a group-balanced subset was the only method that lowered the gap, from 0.18 to 0.01 on average and in 39 of 42 cells (Wilcoxon signed-rank test on cell means, p < 0.001). Task AUROC fell from 0.73 to 0.65. The balanced subset is limited by the rarest (A, Y ) group of the confounded training set and held only 8 to 52 images. A control in Appendix C traces the loss in about equal parts to this small size and to the L1 penalty of the package's DFR head, and none of it to balancing. Its audit score is unchanged by construction, since the embedding is the same. Table C.1 in Appendix C gives the changes in TPR gap and task AUROC of each method for each encoder.

Planted marker.

With the marker on Pneumothorax-positive images at rate 0.5, the conditional probe AUROC for the marker was 0.999, and the probe flagged it in all 10 seeds (largest p = 0.005, Table 11). A head trained with the marker on 0.9 of positive training images used it: on test images, its TPR gap between marked and unmarked images was 0.94 and its FPR gap 0.90.

5.4. CelebA

For A = Male, the conditional probe AUROC was 0.98 given Blond hair, 0.99 given Heavy makeup and 0.98 given Attractive, and all six detectors flagged each task (Table 10). Table 9: Conditional probe AUROC, number of audits with a significant probe (of 63 per attribute: seven encoders, three tasks, 3 seeds), task AUROC and TPR gap of the confounded head before and after each mitigation (package defaults) and its control. Adversarial and contrastive control: same debiasing network and training, mitigation term weight 0. Masking control: the same number of random dimensions set to zero. DFR refits the head only, so its probe columns repeat the raw embedding. Probe columns are computed on the test half of the patients. CheXpert, mean over cells and seeds. Appendix E). The answer to the second question is partial: on CheXpert, encoders with higher conditional probe scores produced heads with larger subgroup gaps when the training data were confounded, with a rank correlation of 0.60 (interval 0.31 to 0.80 when whole encoders are resampled). Within attributes the relation was strong for sex (0.74) and weak for age (0.19). One reason is range restriction: the mean TPR gap of the age cells varied little between cells (SD 0.05, against 0.10 for sex) while seeds within a cell varied by 0.14, so the ranking of age cells is largely seed noise.

For a linear head trained on confounded data, shortcut potential measured on the embedding was therefore informative about use, clearly for sex, not significantly for age. For race, whose potential on CheXpert was weak for every encoder, the heads showed no consistent gap and the relation was not detectable over that range (0.03, Appendix C). It does not establish use. The correlation is across cells, and it was measured for logistic and small MLP heads under one form of confounding, on training sets of 42 to 272 images drawn from a CheXpert sample that is not random. A head trained on unconfounded data showed almost no gap between aligned and misaligned images on the same embeddings. Whether an attribute is used depends on the training data and the head, as Brown et al. [10], Petersen et al. [13] and Kina and Petersen [14] argue. Our aligned and misaligned AUROCs repeat the pattern Kina and Petersen found for a chest-drain shortcut on frozen foundation models.

The mitigation results add a caution: at the package defaults, adversarial and contrastive debiasing lowered the conditional probe score, but the same debiasing networks trained without the mitigation term lowered it nearly as much (for contrastive debiasing the difference from its control was -0.04), and masking the top attribute dimensions did little more than masking random ones. None of the three moved the confounded head's TPR gap by more than 0.01 beyond its control. A head trained on confounded data found the attribute signal that remained. The one method that closed the gap, refitting the head on group-balanced data, left the embedding and its audit score unchanged and cost task AUROC, for reasons unrelated to balancing (Appendix C). Both observations agree with the view that much of shortcut use on frozen encoders is decided in the head [14], and with MEDFAIR's finding that mitigation often does not beat plain training [46]. An audit score can fall for reasons that have nothing to do with debiasing, so a mitigation needs a control, and the head has to be tested.

A positive audit for general-purpose encoders is unsurprising, since encoders pretrained on large image corpora are built to retain most of what is visible. Sex and age leave visible traces in chest radiographs, and earlier work recovered race from chest radiographs, which radiologists cannot do [8, 11], and sex, site and scanner from knee radiographs almost perfectly [12]. For sex in particular, part of the signal is likely anatomical. The audit cannot separate legitimate anatomical information from unwanted information, because both are information about A given Y . Subgroup separability sets an upper limit on harm without implying it [32], and the audit should be read in that sense.

6.2. Relation to earlier findings

Our probe results agree in direction with the encoding of sex, age and race reported by Gichoya et al. and Glocker et al. on full chest X-ray models [8, 11], though our numbers are not directly comparable, because we audit frozen embeddings on small samples and condition on a task. The correlation between audit score and head gap is a frozen-embedding counterpart of the relation Yang et al. reported between demographic encoding and fairness gaps [34]. Dependence measures have so far been used as training penalties [19, 20]. Calibrated by permutation, the same idea also works as a check on a frozen encoder.

6.3. What the secondary detectors add

On this evidence they add very little: their flags rose and fell with the probe's as the effect size changed (effective number 1.5 of 6 over the whole grid, 2.2 at a fixed δ = 0.5), and requiring several of them to agree only cost sensitivity. None of them detected the XOR or variance-shift signals that the probe missed. In the submitted version we read disagreement between detectors as evidence about the geometry of the encoding. Most of that disagreement came from code faults, and the remainder is explained by differences in power. Combining detectors resembles ensembling [63] or a mixture of experts [64], but ensembles gain from roughly independent errors, which these detectors have only in part, and a mixture of experts would need a gate trained on labelled shortcuts. We keep the secondary detectors as diagnostics because their scores are on interpretable scales (fraction of dimensions, centroid distance), and they play no part in the decision.

6.4. Cohorts, acquisition and data handling

Race potential was weak on CheXpert and clearer on MIMIC-CXR. The cohorts differ in task and sampling, and in the make-up of the non-White group, so we do not read this as an institution effect. The clusters followed view and projection on both cohorts, consistent with earlier reports that hospital [6] and scanner [7] signals, and site signals in knee radiographs [12], dominate what image models pick up.

Several of the problems we found were data-handling faults. Repeated images of one patient made every detector reject a meaningless attribute until permutation and folds were grouped by patient. One MIMIC-CXR embedding file did not match its metadata, and the submitted tables reported shortcut flags for it. The CheXpert sex column was inverted in the submitted runs. The first two can be caught cheaply, with a fake-attribute control and a row-alignment check, and we recommend running them before any audit.

7. Limitations

The audit, and every secondary detector, missed the two attribute signals we tested that leave group means unchanged: on the XOR and variance-shift variants no detector did better than chance. The gap lies in the statistics, which are built around differences in location: under the same permutation null, probes on squared coordinates and on pairwise products detected both signals with their calibration intact (Appendix E), and on the clinical cohorts the squared-feature probe changed no decision (Table E.4). A linear probe was a deliberate choice, since it matches how frozen embeddings are usually used, but a nonlinear head could exploit signal that the audit reports as absent. A negative audit is therefore weaker evidence than a positive one.

The audit needs labelled sensitive attributes, which are often missing or recorded as imperfect proxies. It examines one embedding at a time, from one layer of one encoder, and says nothing about other layers or about the encoder after fine-tuning. For age the score was not significantly related to reliance, so on this cohort the audit met its own usefulness criterion clearly for sex only. The head experiment covers two head types (logistic regression and a small multilayer perceptron) and one form of confounding, with two attributes (race, whose signal on CheXpert is weak, only as an additional run in Table C.2) and three tasks on one cohort, and the correlation between audit and reliance is computed across only 42 cells that share encoders. With seven encoders, the interval that resamples them is coarse. The heads pool frontal and lateral views, and on frontal views alone the audit AUROCs moved by at most 0.03.

The CheXpert sample is the first 2,000 images in the order of the official training file, not a random sample, so the CheXpert results may not hold for the full training set and may carry whatever ordering the file was assembled with. Against the full training file the sample has a similar sex and race mix (43% against 41% female, and 64.5% against 63.8% White among images with a recorded race) and slightly younger patients (median age 59 against 62). It also has more lateral views (21% against 14%), which the frontal-only analysis bounds.

The MIMIC-CXR task, in-hospital mortality, is an outcome with many causes outside the image. MIMIC-CXR also has radiological labels, which we did not use as tasks, and the audit's result is specific to the task it conditions on. Both samples are small, which limits power for small groups. The CheXpert race result in particular is rarely detected with 100 or fewer non-White images. Collapsing race into White against non-White hides differences between groups. Records with race unknown, declined or not obtained are left out on both cohorts (217 CheXpert images, 71 MIMIC-CXR subjects). The head-experiment cells are not independent and some are small (42 to 272 training and 60 to 404 test images). The identity of the MIMIC-CXR encoders could not be verified from code. On CheXpert the four re-extracted encoders replaced arrays whose origin is unknown, and the old and new arrays differ (Table F.6). RAD-DINO was pretrained on nearly all the images audited here, and for the other encoders the pretraining data could not be checked image by image. MedSigLIP was trained on medical images paired with reports, MIMIC-CXR among them, so its text side could have taught it findings and demographics that reports mention, and its MIMIC-CXR scores, like RAD-DINO's, may describe an encoder that saw the audited images in pretraining. CheXpert is not among the public data sets its model card lists, and the card does not itemise its licensed data sets.

The Benjamini-Hochberg correction is applied across the five secondary detectors within each cell, and the primary probe is judged at p < 0.05 in each cell, with no adjustment across cells for either. SIS was removed from the score, and methods that need training access were not evaluated. We compared embedding clusters with recorded metadata but did not run an error-aware slice discovery method such as GEORGE or Domino [42, 43], so subgroups on which a head fails without a recorded attribute were not searched for. The mitigations were run only on CheXpert and only at the package defaults, without tuning, so tuned settings could change the result, and the planted marker is a single, simple artefact on one encoder.

8. Conclusion

We asked whether shortcut potential can be measured on a frozen embedding, and whether the measurement predicts how strongly a head trained on that embedding with confounded data relies on the attribute. ShortKit-ML measures the shortcut potential of a frozen embedding for a task with one primary test, a conditional probe calibrated by permuting the attribute within task strata and, where a patient has several images, between patients. The test held its error rate on synthetic data and found a planted marker in every seed, but like every detector here it missed signals that leave group means unchanged, so a negative audit does not rule out a shortcut that a nonlinear head could use.

On CheXpert, its score correlated with how strongly a logistic head trained on confounded data relied on the attribute (Spearman 0.60, 0.74 within sex, not significant within age), but at the package defaults three embedding-level mitigations did no better than their controls at reducing that reliance. Refitting the head on a group-balanced subset closed that gap, in 39 of 42 cells, without changing the audit score. Task AUROC fell because that subset was small and because the package's DFR head uses an L1 penalty. The audit is a first check on an encoder, and the head trained on it has to be tested as well. Two cheap checks caught our own data faults and belong before any audit: a fake patient-level attribute that no detector should find, and a row-alignment check between encoders.

Three extensions would make the audit more useful. Probes on squared and product features found the XOR and variance-shift signals that no detector here found (Appendix E). Making such tests part of the audit, with product features at encoder dimension, is the next step, since on the clinical cohorts the squared probe changed no decision. The link between audit score and reliance should be checked on other cohorts and with larger heads, and under confounding other than a single correlated attribute. Auditing an encoder on images it was pretrained on and on images it never saw would show how much of the potential comes from the pretraining data. The audit is intended as one of the embedding-level checks in DOJO, a community-driven platform for adversarial evaluation of health AI [65].

The wider lesson is about what can be measured. A shortcut can only be audited through an attribute someone recorded, and most of what an encoder has learned from its training data was never recorded. This toolkit is a first step for the case where the attribute is known and the input is a frozen embedding. The harder cases, confounders with no label, signals that no linear test sees, and inputs beyond embeddings (the image itself, text and multimodal encoders) need tools that do not yet exist, and we see this work as a map of which ones to build next. use agreements. The embeddings and metadata needed to rerun the analyses, including the MIMIC-CXR subset and the files it was drawn from, are on a gated Hugging Face dataset (https://huggingface.co/datasets/MITCriticalData/ShortKIT-ML-data), released to credentialed PhysioNet accounts with MIMIC-CXR access; no images are shared. CheXpert embeddings are extracted from pinned public checkpoints by a script in the repository (Table F.6), and the CelebA embeddings by another script there from the public images. The RAD-DINO training image list is published with its model card (https://huggingface.co/microsoft/rad-dino).

Settings used in the head experiment. Adversarial debiasing uses a debiasing network (one linear layer to 64 units, with ReLU and dropout 0.1) followed by a linear task head and, behind a gradient-reversal layer (reversal weight 0.5), a linear adversary. The loss is the sum of the task and adversary crossentropies, trained with Adam (learning rate 10 -3 , batch 64) for 50 epochs. Contrastive debiasing uses the same network. For each anchor it draws up to 32 positives (same Y , other A) and 32 negatives (other Y ), and minimises 0.75 times an InfoNCE loss (temperature 0.05, one term per positive against the negatives) plus 0.25 times the task cross-entropy, with Adam (learning rate 10 -3 ) for 50 epochs. Their controls are the same networks trained on the task loss alone. The contrastive loss in the released package was corrected during the revision: it had treated additional positives of an anchor as negatives. The embedding passed on is the 64-unit output of that network. Shortcut masking and its control are as defined in Section 3.6, applied to the training, test and audit embeddings.

DFR standardises the embedding and refits an L1 logistic head (C = 1, balanced class weights, and the L1 penalty follows the DFR reference implementation [54]) on a subset of the confounded training set with equal numbers of images in each of the four (A, Y ) groups, so it uses 4× the size of the smallest group. To separate the effect of size from that of balancing, we refit the same L1 head on a random subset of the confounded training set of the same size, and an L2 head (as for the confounded head) on the balanced subset, over the same cells and seeds. Task AUROC was 0.65 for DFR, 0.65 for the random subset of the same size, which kept a TPR gap of 0.10 (so the small subset alone removed about half of the confounded head's gap of 0.18), and 0.69 for the balanced subset with the L2 head, against 0.73 for the confounded head. Balancing itself cost no AUROC. The loss came from the small subset and the L1 penalty in about equal parts.

Output shift. The output shift of Section 4.3 correlated negatively with the probe score (-0.26). Projecting out u moves each test embedding by its whole coordinate along u, most of which is spread within each attribute group rather than the gap between groups. The measure therefore tracks how much the head responds to that spread, which is largest for encoders that encode the attribute weakly, so it is reported in Table 8 but not used as a measure of reliance.

Both groups have zero mean in every dimension. Given the partner coordinate, they differ by δ standard deviations.

• Variance shift: attribute dimensions have standard deviation 1 for a i = 0 and 1 + δ for a i = 1, with equal means.

In the submitted version the generator passed the task label as the group, so the synthetic benchmark measured task signal, and the shift was ±δ, which made the effect 2δ. Both are corrected here. Figure E.1 shows the perdimension false positive rate of the statistical detector on null data with and without multiple testing correction.

The blind spot named in Section 7 was checked directly at one small setting of the benchmark (n = 1000, d = 64, ρ = 0.5, K = 200, 50 seeds), without rerunning the grid. The conditional probe was fitted three times on each data set, with the same code and in-fold standardisation, the same folds and the same null (A permuted within Y ). Only the design changed: E (the audit's probe), [E, E 2 ] with the squared coordinates appended, and [E, E 2 , E i E j ] with all d(d -1)/2 pairwise products appended as well (2144 features). Table E.3 gives the rejection rate at p < 0.05 and the mean AUROC.

At δ = 2.0 the squared-coordinate probe rejected the variance shift in 1.00 of runs and the product probe rejected the XOR signal in 1.00 of runs (0.52 at δ = 1.2), while the linear probe stayed at 0.06 on XOR and 0.06 on the variance shift. On null data the three probes rejected in 0.06, 0.04 and 0.06 of runs, so the permutation null calibrates the nonlinear designs as it does the linear one.

Ethics Statement

This study used three publicly available datasets: CheXpert, MIMIC-CXR, and CelebA. CheXpert was released by the Stanford Machine Learning Group under a research data use agreement and consists of deidentified chest radiographs. MIMIC-CXR was released by the Massachusetts Institute of Technology Laboratory for Computational Physiology under the Phys-ioNet Credentialed Health Data License 1.5.0. Access to MIMIC-CXR was obtained through completion of the required CITI Data or Specimens Only Research training (PhysioNet credentialed user). CelebA is a publicly available facial attribute dataset released for academic research. No new human subjects data were collected for this study. As all data used had been collected and deidentified before their release through established public repositories under their respective data use agreements, this work did not require additional institutional review board approval. The study was conducted in accordance with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki.

Declaration of generative AI and AI-assisted technologies in the manuscript preparation process

After using this tool, the authors reviewed and edited the content as needed and take full responsibility for the content of the published article.

Appendix A. Detector definitions

Notation: for each image i, E i ∈ R d is its standardised embedding, with attribute group a i and task label y i . S y = {i : y i = y} is a task stratum and S y,a = {i : y i = y, a i = a} a cell. Statistics averaged over strata are weighted by |S y |. All six statistics are calibrated by the conditional permutation null of Section 3.2. The null recomputes the whole statistic, including any fitted direction, ranking or clustering, on each permuted data set. Conditional probe. L2-regularised logistic regression on [E i , y i ], regularisation strength 1, 5-fold CV stratified on (a, y) and grouped by patient (CheXpert) or identity (CelebA), averaged over five fold splits. Its statistic s is the out-of-fold AUROC for A (macro one-vs-rest when G > 2) [17, 18].

Statistical.

For each dimension j and stratum y, a Mann-Whitney U test (G = 2) or Kruskal-Wallis test (G > 2) of E ij across groups within S y . All d × |Y| p-values are adjusted by Benjamini-Hochberg at 0.05 [51], and s is the fraction of dimensions significant in at least one stratum.

Geometric.

Within stratum y, with group centroids µ y,a , the mean pairwise centroid distance over the pooled within-group spread.

The statistic s is the weighted mean of s y.

Bias direction PCA.

Within stratum y, v y is the first principal component of the group-mean differences (for G = 2, the normalised difference of the two means) [35]. With projections z i = v ⊤ y E i , s y is the largest absolute difference of group means of z divided by the pooled standard deviation of z. Because v y is fitted on the same data, s y is positive even under the null. The permutation null accounts for this, which a fixed threshold did not.

HBAC.

Within stratum y, k-means with k = 8 clusters on E, with s y the normalised mutual information between cluster labels and A [44, 52].

Frequency. Within each training fold, dimensions are ranked by their absolute within-stratum standardised group difference (one ranking per onevs-rest target when G > 2, as for the probe) and the top 5% are kept; s is the out-of-fold AUROC of the conditional probe restricted to those dimensions [53]. The values of k, the top fraction and the probe's C are package defaults fixed before any result was seen and were not tuned. Table F.7 reports the probe's sensitivity to C.

Appendix B. Package methods outside the audit score

The package implements 20 methods. Table 2 covers the six scored detectors and Table 3 shows where each method is used. The remaining 14, and what each needs beyond (E, A, Y ): • Demographic parity, equalized odds, intersectional analysis: a trained classifier's predictions.

Demographic parity is the difference in positive prediction rate between groups, equalized odds the largest difference in TPR or FPR, and intersectional analysis the same gaps over combinations of attributes. They are properties of a trained classifier; of the three, only the equalized-odds gaps (TPR and FPR) are reported in this paper, for the heads of Section 4.3.

• GroupDRO [66], GCE [67], early-epoch clustering (SPARE): training a model and access to its loss or representations during training.

• SSA: a split into attribute-labelled and unlabelled data.

• CAV: user-defined concept examples. SpRAy [68] and GradCAM mask overlap [69]: images and model gradients.

• Causal effect estimation [70, 71], generative CVAE, VAE disentanglement: training an auxiliary model.

• SIS: the current implementation searches for sufficient subsets for the task label, with a fixed subset fraction of 15%. It has no attributeaware form and was removed from the score.

Appendix C. Mitigation method details

1. Shortcut masking: The embedding dimensions with the largest loading on the attribute direction (the top 5% here) are set to zero, randomised or inpainted. The method works on the embeddings themselves and needs no retraining.

2. Background randomisation:

For image-level pipelines, foreground objects are swapped across backgrounds so that background and label are no longer correlated. It needs segmentation masks or a foreground extractor.

3. Adversarial debiasing: Adversarial training with a gradient reversal layer removes group information from the learned representation [72, 73]. An adversary tries to predict A from E, and the debiasing network is trained to raise the adversary's loss while keeping task performance.

4. Explanation regularisation (RRR):

A Right for the Right Reasons regularisation term, added to the training loss, penalises model attention on detected shortcut regions.

5. Last-layer retraining (DFR):

Only the final classification layer is retrained, on a group-balanced subset of the data [54]. The method is cheap to run and suited to the case where the attribute is encoded in the representation and the head gives it too much weight. It leaves the embedding unchanged and, in Section 4.3, lowered the TPR gap at a cost in task AUROC.

6. Contrastive debiasing: A contrastive loss pulls together representations from different demographic groups within the same task class [74], so that the groups become less separable while the task classes stay apart.

Of these, shortcut masking, adversarial debiasing, last-layer retraining and contrastive debiasing work on frozen embeddings. They were run with the package defaults and are evaluated in Section 4.3. Background randomisation and explanation regularisation need images or model gradients and were not evaluated.

Appendix D. Implementation and reproducibility

Seeds, permutation counts, run times and the configuration of every stage are documented in the repository, with the run manifests from which each table and figure was regenerated.

Appendix E. Synthetic benchmark detail

The generator draws y i ∼ Bernoulli(0.5) and sets a i = y i with probability ρ and a i = 1 -y i otherwise. The embedding has d coordinates drawn from N (0, 1). A block of k y = 4 task dimensions is shifted by ±µ y /2 according to y i , with µ y = 1.0. A disjoint block of k a = 4 attribute dimensions carries the attribute signal: • Linear: each attribute dimension is shifted by +δ/2 for a i = 1 and -δ/2 for a i = 0, so the standardised mean difference is exactly δ in each dimension and the Mahalanobis distance over the block is √ k a δ.

Embedding visualisations

An L2 logistic head on standardised embeddings is trained on a subsample with P (Y = 1 | A = 1) = 0.9 and P (Y = 1 | A = 0) = 0.1 (ρ train = 0.9), and tested on a patient-disjoint subsample with all four (A, Y ) groups of equal size (ρ = 0.5). Patients are first split in half, stratified on the image-level (A, Y ) labels with patients as groups (scikit-learn's StratifiedGroupKFold), so every image of a patient falls in one half, with a different split for each seed. The subsamples below draw images within each (A, Y ) cell of a half. In the training half the (A, Y ) groups (1, 1) and (0, 0) each hold 0.45N images and (1, 0) and (0, 1) each hold 0.05N , with N the largest size that the smallest group allows, so N changes with the split. Training sets held 42 to 272 images (24 to 124 patients), and test sets 60 to 404 images (40 to 153 patients).

Detectors and their status in the revised audit. For every statistic s m , larger means more information about A in E given Y . Every scored detector takes only the embedding E, the attribute A and the task label Y , and is calibrated by the conditional permutation null of Section 3.2 (A shuffled within Y strata, K permutations; the probe judged at p < 0.05, Benjamini-Hochberg across the five secondary detectors of a cell). Null FPR: fraction of synthetic data sets with δ = 0 rejected at p < 0.05 before correction, pooled over all settings and 10 seeds. After BH across the five secondary detectors no secondary detector exceeded 0.03 (Table E.1).

Table 4 :

Frozen encoders: architecture, pretraining and embedding dimension. CheXpert uses all seven, and MIMIC-CXR uses RAD-DINO, ViT-B/16, ViT-B/32 and MedSigLIP.Race is White against non-White in the primary analysis, because several groups are small in these samples. A sensitivity analysis tests separately the race groups with at least 50 images (White, Black and Asian on CheXpert, and White and Black on MIMIC-CXR), and repeats this keeping only group and Y combinations with at least 50 images. On CheXpert only White patients reach 50 images with Y = 1, so that version compares groups among Y = 0 images only. Group sizes for every cohort and attribute are given in Table F.4.
